general_technique.text: Move around to find a school: start on the bottom (perch feed mainly there), pull the bait up a few feet if nothing bites, and try a new spot after a few minutes with no strikes. Once found, mark the school's depth with a bobber; schools are usually one size, so move on if only small perch bite.

sources.citation: Wisconsin DNR, Bureau of Fisheries Management. Yellow Perch (Perca flavescens) fact sheet, by Maureen Mecozzi.
sources.quote: Because perch feed primarily near the bottom, start looking for schools there. If you have no success on the bottom, pull your bait up a few feet before moving to a new location because ... If you have no strikes after a few minutes, try a new location. Once you've located a school, mark the depth of the school with a bobber on the line. Since schools usually contain fish of about the same size, if only small perch are biting, look for a school of larger fish.

general_technique.text: Perch nibble rather than strike, so most anglers set the hook with a swift jerk at the slightest nibble; they are notorious bait thieves.

sources.citation: Wisconsin DNR, Bureau of Fisheries Management. Yellow Perch (Perca flavescens) fact sheet, by Maureen Mecozzi.

With such a light bite, most anglers set the hook with a swift jerk at even the slightest indication of a nibble, or they may end up pulling up a bare hook. Perch are notorious bait thieves.

general_technique.text: Fish the bottom - especially by day, when catfish sit in a river's deepest holes (below dams and power plants), which usually means fishing from boats or bridges. At night, fish from riverbanks or backwaters. Wait until the line moves, showing the catfish has fully taken the bait, before setting the hook. Channel catfish fishing is often excellent the first few days after a rain.
